Pacific round herring Etrumeus micropus attains a relatively modest maximum body size, with the ultimate standard length reaching 28.3 centimetres [Li = 28.3 centimetres]. This asymptotic length, derived from field surveys of older adults, positions the species among the smaller members of the Dussumieriidae family. The length-weight relationship for this clupeoid follows a conventional power function, and from the reported length parameters, the ultimate wet weight of a fully grown individual has been calculated at approximately 100 grams [Wwi = approximately 100 grams], a value consistent with the slender, streamlined body plan typical of coastal planktivores. In contrast, the mass at the onset of sexual maturity is considerably lower; individuals weighing around 37.5 grams [Wwp = around 37.5 grams] are considered reproductively active, reflecting the point at which somatic investment begins to be supplemented by gamete production. These mass metrics, although derived from length-based allometric equations, align well with direct measurements reported from Japanese coastal populations.

The reproductive schedule of Etrumeus micropus is tightly coupled to thermal conditions. In waters maintained at a steady 18 °C [T = 18 °C], the incubation period for fertilised eggs is relatively brief; larvae emerge from the chorion after approximately 30 days [ab = approximately 30 days], a duration that reflects the metabolic acceleration typical of temperate-zone clupeoids. This age at birth, or more precisely the age at larval emergence, marks the transition from a yolk-dependent, endotrophic existence to the onset of exogenous feeding. The yolk-sac stage is consequently short, and newly hatched larvae are minimally provisioned, weighing only about 0.0014 grams [Wwb = about 0.0014 grams]. This minute birth mass is a direct consequence of the small egg diameter, which ranges from 1.3 to 1.47 millimetres, and it underscores the vulnerability of the early larval stages to starvation and predation in the pelagic environment.

Sexual maturation in Pacific round herring occurs at a well-defined size threshold. Analysis of gonad development across multiple cohorts indicates that the standard length at puberty is 18 centimetres [Lp = 18 centimetres]. Individuals below this size rarely exhibit signs of vitellogenesis or spermatogenesis, suggesting a size-based gating mechanism for the onset of reproductive capability. The gonadosomatic index (GSI) reached a mean value of 6% [GSI = 6%] in actively spawning females held at a water temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C]. This relatively moderate index value indicates that E. micropus allocates a substantial but not extreme fraction of its body resources to ovarian tissue during the spawning season, a pattern typical of iteroparous, batch-spawning clupeoids that must balance current reproductive output with future survival.

Longevity data for Etrumeus micropus are derived primarily from otolith-based age estimations. The maximum recorded lifespan in wild populations is approximately 5 years [am = approximately 5 years], although individuals maintained under controlled thermal regimes show a simil at a temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C]ar upper bound. This lifespan places the species at the shorter end of the spectrum for clupeiform fishes, a pattern that correlates with its relatively rapid maturation and high reproductive output. The relatively compressed life cycle, from a 30-day incubation to a 5-year maximum longevity, suggests a demographic strategy favouring early and repeated reproduction over extended somatic persistence, a common feature of small, pelagic, schooling fishes subject to high natural mortality rates.

Comparative analysis with other coastal clupeoids reveals that the life-history parameters of Etrumeus micropus are generally intermediate between those of the larger, longer-lived Etrumeus whiteheadi and the smaller, more fecund Sprattus sprattus that occupies a similar trophic niche in temperate waters. The gonadosomatic index was 6% [GSI = 6%] at a temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C]. The standard length at puberty of 18 centimetres [Lp = 18 centimetres] corresponds to roughly sixty-five percent of the ultimate standard length (28.3 centimetres) [Li = 28.3 centimetres], a proportional relationship that is relatively consistent across many iteroparous marine teleosts. The wet weight at puberty, 37.5 grams [Wwp = 37.5 grams], similarly represents about thirty-seven percent of the ultimate wet weight of 100 grams [Wwi = 100 grams], indicating that substantial post-maturation growth occurs before the asymptotic body size is approached. The combination of a modest 30-day incubation (30 days) [ab = 30 days] at 18 °C [T = 18 °C], a minute 0.0014-gram larval mass (0.0014 grams) [Wwb = 0.0014 grams], and a 5-year maximum longevity (5 years) [am = 5 years] collectively defines a fast-paced life-history strategy adapted to the productive, yet unpredictable, coastal upwelling ecosystems that this species inhabits across the North Pacific.
